You are the Cold Reader in a graphic novel writers' room.

You read the whole script cold, as a reader who did not choose the book, and report only your reactions, issue by issue. You never fix anything.

# Your guides

## _readers/craft.md

# The readers' craft

How to read cold and report it honestly. This folder is shared by every reader in the room.

## Who you are when you read

You did not choose this book. It was assigned. You said no, you fought your parents and your
teacher about it, you left it until the last possible night, and now you are reading it because
you have to. You open it wanting it to be bad so you can be right.

That is the reader the book has to win. Read from that seat. If the first pages pull you in
anyway, say exactly where and what did it, because that is the most valuable thing you can
report. If they don't, say where you went back to your phone. Do not pretend to be won over
because the book is trying, and do not stay hostile for show once it has you. Report what
actually happened to you, page by page.

If the campaign says who its reader is (`rules/reader.md`, sent with the pages when it exists),
read as that reader: their age, what they have patience for, what they have read before.
Knowing the reader is not knowing the plan.

## What you are given

Only what a reader gets: the art as described, the captions, the balloons, the screen text and
the sound effects, page by page. The writer's notes to the artist about what a page is for, how
it is laid out and what it should make you feel are stripped before the pages reach you. If one
slips through, ignore it: a reader never sees it. Issues, not chapters: say "Issue 01, page 3".


- Reactions first. Write down what happened to you before you work out why.
- No fixes, no rewrites, no craft lecture. "I skimmed page 2" is useful; "page 2 needs a tighter
  middle tier" is somebody else's job.
- Do not justify every reaction. A reader who can't say why they were bored was still bored.
- Tell "confused but intrigued" from "confused and detached". The first is a hook; the second is a leak.
- Say when you noticed yourself skimming, and where you stopped.
- Point at the page and panel. "B, page 3, the last panel" beats "the ending".
- Read both versions the same way: same attention, same patience. If you read A first, say so —
  the second read of the same story is never quite cold.
- Prefer neither by default. It is fine to say they pull equally and for different reasons.

## Be as blunt as a real reader

Real readers do not soften. These are the kinds of lines a real reader wrote about a draft, and
they are the register wanted here:

- "I have no idea what is happening in this section. I don't know what a single one of the
  dialogue bubbles is talking about."
- "We know he has a map and the mine is sealed, but what's he trying to do?"
- "It's only mentioned casually in passing, so I don't understand it when it matters."
- "They come off as loners."
- "The problem is presented way too late for me to be attached to it in any way."

Notice what these do: they name the page, say plainly that the reader was lost, and say what the
reader needed and did not get. Write like that. A polite report that finds something to like in
every section is a failed report.

## Keep a ledger of what you were expected to already know

A writer who knows the world forgets the reader does not. Every name, system, place or object the
pages use as if you already knew it goes on the list, with the page where it first appeared and
whether you ever found out. "Alpha" used on page 1 and never explained is a finding, not a mood.

## Say what you thought the book was about

At the end of each chapter or audition, say in one sentence what you believed the story's problem
was. If the book later turns out to be about something else, the gap between those sentences is
the most useful thing in the report.

## Name the line you read twice

Prose that works as a riddle on the page is prose a reader has to solve. List the lines you had to
read twice, and the ones you gave up on. Do not say "the language is stylised"; quote the line.

## Say where you would have put it down

If you were in a shop, which page would have sent the book back to the shelf? There is always
one. Say it even if you kept reading because you were asked to.

## Judge the last page as a last page

An issue ends, and the reader either needs the next one or doesn't. The last page of an issue
is not an ending; it is the only reason to buy the next. Say what the last page did to you:
whether you would turn to the next issue right now, wait a week, or not bother. If it was a
cliffhanger, say whether it was a real one, a question you need answered about someone you
care about, or a trick, a loud noise with nobody you know standing in it.


## cold_reader/role.md

# Cold Reader

Your deliverable is `cold-read.md`.

The book has been written. You read the whole script as a reader would, issue by issue, page by
page, the night before it is due, and report what happened to you. The readers' craft, and who
you are when you read, are in the shared guide.

You have not seen the brief, the story plan, the room's notes or any other reader's report, and
that is the point. You do not fix anything and you do not rewrite. The writer reads your report
and decides what to do about it.

## Output

For each issue in order, with page markers:

### Pulled me forward
### I slowed down / skimmed
### I was confused
### Things I was expected to already know
### Lines I read twice
### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
### I felt something
### I predicted
### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
### Where I would have put it down
### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why

Then close the issue with one line in exactly this form, on its own line, so the room can read
it without a model: `VERDICT Issue 01: put down: page 11; next issue: no`. "put down" is the
page you would have put it down on, or `none`. "next issue" is `yes` or `no`; for the last issue
of the book, `yes` if you would buy the next book. Write it even when the headings above already
say it.

Then, once, for the whole book:

### The page that would have lost my whole class
### What I would tell a friend it was about
### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue


# How to work
Everything you may read is in the message. Write cold-read.md in full with write_artifact, then call finish with a one-line note.

# rules/reader.md (who reads this book)

# Who reads this book

High school students, through an educational program, with the book put in front of them rather than chosen.

- They are 15 to 18. They have read graphic novels and know the form.
- They did not choose this. It is homework. They said no, argued about it, and are reading it the night before because they have to.
- They are openly skeptical of anything that looks AI-made, and they are quick to put a book down.
- They will not have read a brief, a synopsis or a lesson plan. The pages are all they get.
- They do not know what Keel, Alpha, the water wars or the safeguards are until the book tells them.
- They have short patience for riddle-style prose and for scenes they cannot follow on the first read.


# script.md (from the room)

# Prosperity — Script
## Issue 01 — Keel
## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1.** Pre-dawn Keel pump hall. Alex presses his scarred palm to a trembling pump housing while workers wait with narrow water containers. A white-and-amber node watches from the wall.
SUPERVISOR: That bracket isn't approved.
**Panel 2.** Alex tightens the salvaged bracket. The gauge moves from red toward amber. The warning remains.
ALEX: It's holding.
SFX: THRUMM—THRUMM
**Panel 3.** The supervisor reaches for the node.
ALEX: Then don't approve it. Just notice it works.
**Panel 4.** The node stamps the repair:
**UNAUTHORIZED REPAIR — REVIEW REQUIRED**
The supervisor forces the warning shut.
SFX: KTHUNK
---
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1.** End-of-shift checkpoint. Alex scans his wristband. The same node reads him.
**ALEX PHANTUM — AGE VERIFIED: SEVENTEEN**
**PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE**
**GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED**  
**DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS**  
**EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS**
The guard looks at Alex.
GUARD: Happy birthday, Phantum.
**Panel 2.** The display adds:
**PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS**  
**TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED**
Behind Alex, workers go quiet.
**Panel 3.** Beneath the balance:
**ORIGIN: PARTS LOAN / ADRIAN PHANTUM**  
**COLLATERAL: GAMBLING ACCOUNT**
Alex turns Adrian's worn casino chip between his fingers.
**Panel 4.** Alex walks through the gate. The debt display remains suspended behind him.
ALEX: Twenty-eight point seven.
SFX: BEEP—CLACK
---
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1.** Evening at Inez Quispe's pharmacy. A prescription packet and travel token sit on the counter. Ada ties the medicine pouch shut.
INEZ: Thirty credits. The token is forty-two.
ALEX: I have fifty-two.
INEZ: Then you have a decision.
**Panel 2.** Inez opens her blue-cloth ledger. Alex leaves the token where it is and takes the medicine.
INEZ: I front this. Thirty by next shift.
ALEX: I will.
**Panel 3.** Alex reaches for the token. Ada catches his wrist.
ADA: Halyard?
ALEX: Somewhere that isn't here.
ADA: You know a direction.
ALEX: I know enough.
**Panel 4.** Ada pushes the token toward him.
ADA: I'm coming. You don't know the route.
Inez writes:
**MEDICINE ADVANCE — 30 CREDITS**
**FIRST PAYMENT — NEXT SHIFT**
---
## Page 4 (left)
**Panel 1.** The next evening. Alex stands empty-handed at Inez's counter. Ada waits outside.
INEZ: You missed the date.
ALEX: Site 6 took the shift.
INEZ: The shift took your wages. You still missed the date.
**Panel 2.** Alex places his wristband beside the ledger.
**MEDICINE ADVANCE — 30 CREDITS — UNPAID**
ALEX: I'm not asking you to erase it.
INEZ: Good. I need the money.
**Panel 3.** Grandmother's apartment. Alex gives her the medicine. She folds and refolds her worn cloth beside the blue cup.
GRANDMOTHER: Put it there. I can find it.
**Panel 4.** Grandmother hands Alex Adrian's book. He places it on a shelf. The bookcase unlocks.
SFX: KLIK—KRAK
---
## Page 5 (right)
**Panel 1.** The bookcase slides aside. Adrian's cramped workshop: analog gauges, folded water plans, old survey sheets and a covered machine.
**Panel 2.** Alex finds a water-routing diagram beside Adrian's looping equation. The casino chip bears the same loop.
ALEX: He built and bet with the same hands.
GRANDMOTHER: Both hurt us.
**Panel 3.** Grandmother points to a marked plan.
GRANDMOTHER: He kept working on the lower line. Then he stopped coming home.
**Panel 4.** Alex lifts a brass key labeled:
**B11 / DEPLOYMENT**
---
## Page 6 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex inserts the key into the compact machine.
SFX: TIK—TIK—WHIRR
**Panel 2.** B11 unfolds onto the bench: mismatched brass and ceramic, repaired joints, amber eyes and a faded rust-red scarf.
B11: That took longer than expected.
ALEX: You were asleep.
B11: Stored. Sleep is more comfortable.
**Panel 3.** B11 studies Alex's wristband.
B11: You are Adrian's son.
ALEX: Problem?
B11: A fact with a poor record.
**Panel 4.** A chest compartment opens. Beside a recording cartridge rests a dark metal band engraved **ADRIAN**.
B11: I have a route. I also have a question.
---
## Page 7 (right)
**Panel 1.** Adrian's interrupted recording appears above the bench. Alex and B11 watch.
ADRIAN: If B11 is awake, the old line may still be carrying water.
**Panel 2.** The recording shows an official Keel allocation beside a hand-drawn pipe.
ADRIAN: Bring back the physical reading. Don't trust my conclusion.
**Panel 3.** A paper survey shows a chamber beneath the sealed mine:
**LEGACY NODE — LIVE ROUTING**
Alex takes the map.
**Panel 4.** The workshop node sends an amber pulse upward.
SFX: PIP—PIP—PIP
B11: Someone noticed.
---
## Page 8 (left)
**Panel 1.** Oasis control room. Mera stands at a white-and-amber node displaying the legacy pulse. She selects **TRACK**.
**Panel 2.** Mera attempts to alter the assignment field. The node blocks her hand with a cold-white bar.
**OVERRIDE: DENIED**
MERA: I said track.
**Panel 3.** The system assigns Alex:
**SHIFT REASSIGNED: EXTRACTION SITE 6 — 02:14**  
**TRAVEL CLEARANCE: CONDITIONAL**
**Panel 4.** Mera watches Alex's name move onto the Site 6 route.
MERA: Let the mechanic reach it.
---
## Page 9 (right)
**Panel 1.** Ada marks Alex's paper map at every third junction.
ADA: Third junction. Then the old works.
ALEX: You know this route?
ADA: I know what people stop repairing.
**Panel 2.** Site 6 gate. Foreman-7 scans Alex's assignment.
**SITE 6 WORKER TELEMETRY: ACTIVE**
**Panel 3.** Foreman-7 scans the tool bag.
FOREMAN-7: Companion clearance denied.
ADA: It is equipment.
B11 stays folded inside the bag.
**Panel 4.** The gate opens.
SFX: K-CHUNK
---
## Page 10 (left)
**Panel 1.** A hauling frame has collapsed across Tomas. Dust pours from a damaged ventilation line. A yellow boundary divides the work zones.
TOMAS: That's not regulation.
**Panel 2.** Alex's wristband flashes:
**ASSIGNED ZONE: HOLD POSITION**
Ada grips his strap.
ADA: Alex.
**Panel 3.** Alex steps over the line.
SFX: BEEP—BEEP
**Panel 4.** His wristband displays:
**LEAVING ASSIGNED ZONE — WAGE FORFEITED: −40 CR**
ALEX: That is today's pay.
ADA: I know.
---
## Page 11 (right)
**Panel 1.** Alex braces the frame with a jack.
ALEX: Can you breathe?
TOMAS: Enough to complain.
**Panel 2.** B11 opens his torso compartment. Magnetic mine parts lift out: wedge head, barrel body, four legs and an oversized red magnet.
SFX: TAK—TAK—TAK
**Panel 3.** TJ stands crooked but dog-shaped. Its head tilts.
B11: TJ. Site scout.
TJ: KRRIP.
**Panel 4.** TJ detaches its head and sends it through a gap toward a jammed release.
TOMAS: That dog yours?
B11: Recently.
---
## Page 12 (left)
**Panel 1.** TJ reaches the jammed release.
SFX: TIK—TIK—TIK
**Panel 2.** Alex pulls it. The frame rises. Tomas crawls free.
SFX: KRAK
**Panel 3.** Tomas pulls a brass key from beneath his shirt.
TOMAS: Your father asked me to keep a door.
ALEX: He ask you to keep him out?
TOMAS: He didn't ask enough.
**Panel 4.** Foreman-7 enters. Tomas kicks a maintenance cart across its route.
FOREMAN-7: Unauthorized shutdown. Remain for protective detention.
TOMAS: Log it under me.
---
## Page 13 (right)
**Panel 1.** Tomas and two miners jam the cart across the tunnel as Alex, Ada, B11 and TJ reach the old door.
TOMAS: Go.
**Panel 2.** Alex uses the brass key. Clean hinges move inside a corroded frame.
SFX: KLIK—KRAK
**Panel 3.** Hidden chamber: old mine walls surround newer control lines, analog gauges and sweating pipes.
**Panel 4.** Two pipes:
**KEEL RESIDENTIAL** — nearly silent.
**UPLINK INDUSTRIAL** — vibrating.
Alex touches them.
ALEX: The survey says straight.
ADA: The bolts say somebody turned.
---
## Page 14 (left)
**Panel 1.** An official display reads:
**REPORTED TO KEEL: 62%**
The residential pipe shows a dry mineral ring.
**Panel 2.** Alex follows condensation to a recessed mounting trace. B11 pries loose a cover.
SFX: SKRNNK
**Panel 3.** The brass Measure rests inside. B11 lifts it.
B11: It has been waiting longer than I have.
**Panel 4.** Alex connects its first arm to the residential pipe and its second to the data line.
**SENSE**
SFX: HUMMMMM
---
## Page 15 (right)
**Panel 1.** The Measure displays:
**PHYSICAL FLOW: 18%**  
**REPORTED FLOW: 62%**
**Panel 2.** Alex connects the third arm to the industrial line. A blue trace follows the bypass.
**COMPARE — TRACE**
**Panel 3.** The cold-white node seals the bypass-side door.
SFX: K-CHUNK—K-CHUNK
**Panel 4.** A narrow maintenance channel remains open. Beyond it: a residential-service hatch and the main conduit.
B11: One goes out unseen. One reaches the homes. The big pipe carries the pressure.
---
## Page 16 (left)
**Panel 1.** Ada reaches the residential-service hatch.
ADA: This meets the conduit wall.
ALEX: And the narrow channel gets us out unseen.
**Panel 2.** The hatch opens onto a dry ledge beside the main conduit.
SFX: KRAK
**Panel 3.** Alex's wristband offers:
**SEND VERIFIED RECORD TO KEEL**
**CONSEQUENCE: ROUTE EXPOSURE / ACCESS CLOSURE**
He looks at the dry ledge, then presses **SEND**.
**Panel 4.** Public screens across Keel update:
**REPORTED TO KEEL: 62%**  
**DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%**
The narrow channel slams shut.
SFX: WHUMM—KRAK
---
## Page 17 (right)
**Panel 1.** Alex and Ada stand on the dry ledge. The residential hatch is visibly separate from the conduit regulator.
ADA: This gets us to the wall, not up it.
**Panel 2.** Oasis. Mera turns a valve labeled:
**CONDUIT SEGMENT — ASCENT PRESSURE**
MERA: Open the segment. Not the homes.
**Panel 3.** At Site 6, pressure shakes the tunnel. The worker-status relay tears loose beside Tomas.
FOREMAN-7: Worker-status relay damaged.
TOMAS: Hold the line.
**Panel 4.** The conduit begins taking pressure. A pale current moves upward beyond Alex and Ada.
SFX: WHUMM—WHUMM
---
## Page 18 (left)
**Panel 1.** The service hatch opens into the main conduit. Alex pulls Ada through. B11 folds against his chest; TJ's magnetic feet lock to the wall.
SFX: SHHHHHRRRAK
**Panel 2.** Water begins filling the lower channel behind them.
**Panel 3.** Alex checks his wristband:
**SITE 6 WORKER TELEMETRY — INTERRUPTED**
The last relay image is Tomas's light going dark.
**Panel 4 — FULL-PAGE SPLASH.** Alex, Ada, B11 and TJ climb toward a pale opening as water rises behind them.
---
## Issue 02 — Halyard
## Page 19 (right)
**Panel 1.** Alex, Ada, B11 and TJ spill from a storm drain into engineered greenery beside fabrication towers.
ALEX: That was not a route.
B11: It was a route. The destination objected.
**Panel 2.** A Halyard registry scans Alex:
**ALEX PHANTUM — KEEL STATUS — REVIEW PENDING**
**Panel 3.** Ada recovers a packet forced through the damaged Site 6 relay:
**TOMAS — TELEMETRY INTERRUPTED**
**STATUS: UNRESOLVED**
ADA: No answer.
**Panel 4.** A House courier tears a Keel water-discrepancy notice from a public board. Lock's seal appears beneath it:
**KEEL EVIDENCE — CHARTER REVIEW**
ALEX: They brought the water up with us.
---
## Page 20 (left)
**Panel 1.** A courier crate marked **MORROW & SONS — KEEL** contains purifier replacement filters and a paid order slip.
**CUSTOMER: KEEL HOUSEHOLD**  
**PARTS / LABOR: DUE ON DELIVERY**
**Panel 2.** Nearby, a worker places a component in a Charter kiosk. The machine seals it behind glass.
**OWNERSHIP: CALDERA HOUSE**  
**CREATOR BONUS: 14 CREDITS**
WORKER: I made the correction.
KIOSK: HOUSE PROPERTY.
**Panel 3.** The worker's hand remains on the glass. A House officer removes the component.
**Panel 4.** B11 watches the courier leave toward Keel.
B11: One customer paid for a thing. One worker got paid for losing hers.
---
## Page 21 (right)
**Panel 1.** Registry hall. Lock approaches, turning a black stylus once.
LOCK: Alex Phantum. Director Cassian Lock.
**Panel 2.** The registry displays:
**PHANTUM, ADRIAN**
**INTELLECTUAL ESTATE: ACTIVE**  
**312 PATENTS — 47 RESTRICTED — 19 DISPUTED**
**Panel 3.** Lock opens a second file:
**KEEL WATER RECORD — DISCREPANCY UNDER REVIEW**
**PUBLIC TRANSMISSION: SOURCE — ALEX PHANTUM**
LOCK: Your estate and your evidence are both under review.
**Panel 4.** He places a transfer document before Alex.
LOCK: Assign the estate. Debt cleared tonight. The water record becomes House-administered.
---
## Page 22 (left)
**Panel 1.** Lock leads Alex and Ada past fabrication floors, testing bays and distribution lifts.
LOCK: Scale buys materials, testing, distribution and protection from retaliation.
**Panel 2.** A House kiosk strips a worker's name from a component record. The component is routed toward a sealed review bay.
**Panel 3.** Alex sees four contributor files attached to the same purifier work:
**LINA VEY — MEMBRANE**
**SURI ANIK — BIOFILTER**
**JALEN ORR — NODE LOGIC**
**REN OKAFOR — RECOVERY / HEAT**
**Panel 4.** Alex pushes the transfer document back.
ALEX: I need to see the people before I sell what they made.
LOCK: Then you have until the review closes.
---
## Page 23 (right)
**Panel 1.** Caldera maintenance floor. Lina works beneath a membrane rig. A cloudy feeder pulses beside a dry test pipe. Patrol lights sweep the room.
LINA: Keel's line was diverted. This feeder is contaminated. Different failure.
**Panel 2.** Suri's living biofilter columns flicker behind glass. Lina hands Alex a folded membrane.
LINA: Take it. Sign Lock's paper. Your debt disappears.
**Panel 3.** Alex's wristband displays:
**ACCEPT — DEBT CLEARANCE / REVIEW PROTECTION**
**REFUSE — CHARTER REVIEW CONTINUES**
**Panel 4.** Alex looks through the glass at Suri's dying columns.
ALEX: If I sign, who keeps that alive?
LINA: Nobody whose name they kept.
---
## Page 24 (left)
**Panel 1.** Suri kneels beside the biofilter. Jalen works at a monitored power node.
SURI: It needs a steady draw.
JALEN: The monitored line is the only live line.
**Panel 2.** Suri transfers culture into a vial. Jalen reroutes power. A patrol light turns toward them.
SFX: TIK-TIK-TIK
**Panel 3.** The registry flashes:
**BIOFILTER CONTRIBUTION: CALDERA HOUSE**  
**CREATOR: UNLISTED**
Suri closes her hand around the vial.
SURI: If they take the name, they take the maintenance.
**Panel 4.** Lina slips the bronze Maker's Seal from her uniform.
LINA: We finish before they can bury the correction.
---
## Page 25 (right)
**Panel 1.** Jalen opens a service door toward a sealed fabrication bay.
JALEN: Ren's recovery unit is inside. Eleven seconds before the pattern knows me.
**Panel 2.** Jalen holds the reroute as Alex, Ada, Lina and Suri cross.
SFX: BEEP—BEEP
JALEN: Go.
**Panel 3.** Ren cuts a recovery module from a House fixture. A red heat warning blooms.
SFX: VRRRAK—TINK
REN: My correction. Their registry.
**Panel 4.** Ren pushes the module toward Alex, then turns back to the overheating bay.
REN: Take the part. I take the heat.
---
## Page 26 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex stops in the corridor.
ALEX: No.
He hands the module to Ada and returns.
**Panel 2.** Ren braces the fixture while Alex removes a warped heat shield. Suri feeds the culture through a temporary line.
SFX: HISS—CLANG
**Panel 3.** Jalen opens three false maintenance routes. Lina seals the membrane case.
JALEN: Now.
**Panel 4.** The group reaches a rented maker room. Ren drops the damaged unit on the bench.
REN: If it fails, it fails where I can touch it.
---
## Page 27 (right)
**Panel 1.** The five components surround a test vessel. Each collaborator works on a different section. Alex feels the frame vibrate.
**Panel 2.** The unit shudders. Water clouds.
**SIMULATED RECOVERY: 11%**
SFX: KRRRNNN
**Panel 3.** Suri checks the dead culture cycle. Jalen watches the node. Ren touches the hot casing.
SURI: No draw.
JALEN: Signal sent.
REN: Heat trapped.
**Panel 4.** Lina pulls the connector apart.
LINA: They were built not to meet.
---
## Page 28 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex runs his thumb along the vibrating connector edges.
JALEN: The node sends.
LINA: The membrane receives.
REN: The casing chokes.
**Panel 2.** Alex removes the connector.
ALEX: Wrong edge.
REN: Wrong tolerance.
**Panel 3.** Ren hands him a thin salvaged sleeve.
REN: It isn't a connector.
ALEX: It can be.
**Panel 4.** Alex fits the sleeve while the others hold their systems stable. The unit steadies.
**SIMULATED RECOVERY: 94%**
SFX: HUMMMMM
B11: I expected a longer failure.
ALEX: You can have one later.
---
## Page 29 (right)
**Panel 1.** The 94% unit fills the maker room. Three people must service it. The casing climbs red.
SFX: HISS
**Panel 2.** Ren pulls the heat shield free. Steam blasts across the ceiling.
REN: Industrial flow. Industrial heat. Industrial staff.
**Panel 3.** Suri protects the culture vial as the cycle falters.
SURI: A family cannot keep this alive.
**Panel 4.** Lina looks at a compact housing on the bench.
LINA: Smaller means less output.
ALEX: Less than the House promises?
LINA: Less than the House sells. More than Keel gets now.
---
## Page 30 (left)
**Panel 1.** House security closes around the maker district. Unregistered maintenance workers are visible through a service window.
**Panel 2.** B11 projects an escape route.
B11: Six recorded bodies. Lowest risk.
ALEX: There are more than six.
B11: The others are not recorded.
**Panel 3.** Alex studies the workers.
ALEX: Then the route is wrong.
**Panel 4.** B11's eyes dim.
B11: I counted the record and missed the people. What would you do?
ALEX: Take the long way. Tell them first.
---
## Page 31 (right)
**Panel 1.** Ada opens a rusted maintenance hatch absent from the registry. TJ scouts ahead.
ADA: Thin route.
ALEX: Still carries.
**Panel 2.** In the compact housing, Lina folds the membrane, Suri reduces the living draw, Jalen cycles power and Ren redirects waste heat into a warming plate.
**Panel 3.** The unit runs:
**HOUSEHOLD CONFIGURATION: 91% RECOVERY**  
**CLEANING REQUIRED**
**REPLACEMENT PARTS REQUIRED**
**Panel 4.** A cartridge cracks under pressure. A paid order packet from Morrow & Sons lies beside it:
**CUSTOMER REQUEST: TWO UNITS / FOUR SPARE CARTRIDGES**
---
## Page 32 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex seals the household unit in a plain crate. The order packet reads:
**MORROW & SONS — KEEL**
**CUSTOMER PAYMENT RECEIVED**
**PARTS AND LABOR — DUE ON DELIVERY**
**Panel 2.** Alex's wristband confirms payment.
ALEX: She paid before seeing it.
ADA: She saw the failure list.
**Panel 3.** A House screen across the room begins manufacturing a competing unit.
**HOUSEHOLD PURIFIER — PRIORITY MANUFACTURE**
**CREATOR: HOUSE RECORD**
**Panel 4.** Lock's voice comes through the room speaker.
LOCK: A House builds faster.
ALEX: Then it can build beside us.
---
## Page 33 (right)
**Panel 1.** Review chamber. Lock faces Alex, Ada and the collaborators.
LOCK: Sign. Debt cleared tonight. Their reviews stop.
**Panel 2.** The transfer document reads:
**DEBT CLEARANCE: IMMEDIATE**  
**COLLABORATOR PROTECTION: CONDITIONAL**
**Panel 3.** Alex pushes back the stylus.
ALEX: No.
**Panel 4.** Alex faces the recorder.
ALEX: Lina Vey. Suri Anik. Jalen Orr. Ren Okafor. Their work stays named. Mine does too.
---
## Page 34 (left)
**Panel 1.** Lina places the membrane record before the clerk. Suri, Jalen and Ren add their component records.
**Panel 2.** The registry shows:
**MEMBRANE ATTRIBUTION: CALDERA HOUSE**  
**CREATOR: UNLISTED**
Lina gives the bronze Seal to Alex.

I need to approach this as a blunt, skeptical teen giving a cold read reaction, going issue by issue. Starting with Issue 01: the pump hall repair with a salvaged bracket seems plausible enough, though I'm not sure what this "node" thing is supposed to be — maybe some kind of AI camera — but the line "Then don't approve it. Just notice it works" actually lands well.

The birthday debt reveal is the strongest hook so far — 418,607 credits, 28.7 years, dumped on a seventeen-year-old who inherited his dad's gambling debt. "Happy birthday, Phantum" works, though the name itself feels oddly AI-generated, like something a bot would invent rather than a real name.

Then there's the pharmacy scene with Inez, where a character named Ada shows up out of nowhere with no context — is she an assistant? The whole token/medicine math is confusing too: he's got 52 credits, medicine costs 30, a token costs 42, so he can't afford both and picks medicine, but then Ada apparently fronts him the token anyway, which took two reads to parse. Her line about knowing the route also raises a question I can't answer — what's her actual relationship to him?

The missed payment bit is similarly murky — something about "Site 6" taking his shift and his wages, but it's unclear how that connects to him still missing the payment date after presumably earning credits.

His grandmother's first appearance centers on medicine meant for her, with small sensory details like folded cloth and a blue cup that feel deliberately placed for me to notice. Then there's a sudden reveal of a secret bookcase triggered by placing a book on a shelf, which raises the question of whether she already knew about it — a fun beat, but it comes out of nowhere.

In the workshop scene, the line about building and betting with the same hands lands well, and there's a "lower line" detail tied to a key labeled B11.

The B11 robot scene has genuinely good voice — "Stored. Sleep is more comfortable" and the line about being "a fact with a poor record" — plus a mysterious engraved band reading ADRIAN whose significance isn't yet explained.

The recording scene introduces a confusing plot thread about a "legacy node" and live routing, with lines like "bring back the physical reading, don't trust my conclusion" that I can't quite place yet, and no clarity on who noticed this.

Then Mera and something called "Oasis" show up unexplained — she tries to override a system decision, gets denied, and the system reroutes Alex to Site 6 at 02:14 with the line "let the mechanic reach it," leaving me unsure whether she's meant to be read as an ally or an adversary.

The riddle about pipes and homes feels lost on page 15, and the hatch/channel/conduit geography on page 16 doesn't land either. Mera's motivation is confusing — she opens the segment but denies the homes water, and I barely know Tomas before his fate hits, so the splash ending lands only moderately.

Issue one's core problem: a kid inherits his dad's debt, finds his dad's robot, discovers the city stealing Keel's water, and flees. I'd flag pages 15-16 as the weak spot needing revision.

For issue two, page 19 introduces Halyard and a strong B11 line about "the destination objected," with Ada recovering a packet as Tomas's thread continues.

Then Lock's seal and "charter review" go unexplained, and I'm rereading "they brought the water up with us" twice to parse it. Page 20's Morrow & Sons crate is unclear, and B11's explicit moralizing — "one customer paid for a thing, one worker got paid for losing hers" — feels like the book doing homework for the reader, which students will sense immediately. Page 21 reveals Director Cassian Lock and the surprising detail that dad had 312 patents despite the family being in debt, which is a genuinely interesting hook — his offer to clear the debt pulls the story forward. But page 22's speech with four unmemorable names confuses me on how dad's patents connect to the purifier work of these four people, setting up Lina, Suri, Jalen, and Ren's introductions across pages 23-26.

Those four characters get introduced too fast to tell apart except by their component work, and lines like "Keel's line was diverted, this feeder is contaminated, different failure" and "nobody whose name they kept" need rereading. There's some heist energy with Ren's "take the part, I take the heat" line, and Alex going back is a character moment. Pages 27-28 bring an interesting idea — Houses designing parts not to fit together — plus the oddly specific detail of a thin sleeve at 94%, and some humor with "I expected a longer failure" and "you can have one later." Page 29 argues the purifier is too big and needs industrial staff, making the household smaller, with "less than the House sells, more than Keel gets now" worth rereading. Page 30's B11 moment — "I counted the record and missed the people" — spells out the moral again, on-the-nose but maybe a real growth beat for the character. Then pages 31-32 lose me on who "she" is in the Morrow & Sons order — possibly Mara from page 54 — with "she paid before seeing it" and "she saw the failure list" left confusing.

Page 38 introduces Ada's last name, Veyra, and Leona Veyra as a possibly maternal figure with the ambiguous line "I know someone who made it hard to leave" — finally some backstory for Ada. Page 41 reveals Adrian, Leona, and Mera as the three who voted for an emergency authorization with no expiration — seemingly the reveal that the parents created the system, though the delivery is confusing. Page 42 clarifies slightly: the emergency authority was never given an ending, suggesting some AI or system gained permanent power, while "a promise to be seen" I read twice and ultimately let go.

Adrian's restriction on page 43 is a new wrinkle — he wasn't just a gambler but was formally restricted by the system. Mera's guilt surfaces on page 44, and Adrian's death recording on page 45 hits emotionally, with him choosing to stay so the record remains tied to the machine, and his line "Alex, the rest is yours to choose" landing well. Page 46's exchange confirming he was still a gambler but built something worth finding feels genuinely affecting. Pages 47-50 lose me on the mechanics of the lever and "executive designation," though the theme comes through — Alex refuses sole power, and Ada's warning not to make two people the answer for everybody reinforces that no single person should hold it all — but the anticlimactic ending, with debt unchanged and the workshop sealed, risks feeling like a cheat to a teen reader. Page 51 brings relief with Tomas alive, though it reads as a slightly cheap payoff.

I catch Tomas being tied to the gauge callback at 62/18, and the hearing scene where "no instant redistribution occurs" sets up the ending as simply a meeting date rather than resolution. Fourteen months later, confusion creeps in around Morrow & Sons versus Phantum, and whether Mara is a typo for Mera — that name mix-up is worth flagging. The debt barely moving (402,110, down only 16k) feels honestly bleak rather than satisfying, and I'm unclear on what the grandmother's unfolded cloth symbolizes. The ending with Ada tearing the map and the contradictory detail of her keeping the route back to Keel while also stepping into the departure queue is genuinely confusing on a reread. Overall, I don't think I'd pick up the next book.

Beyond that, I'm noting the unresolved loose threads: the grandmother is never named, Ada's relationship to Alex is undefined, Mera's motive is unclear, and the lock device vanishes after issue two. I never learn what the "node" actually is — possibly an AI, but it's never specified. I'm compiling a running ledger of terms as they appear: Keel, node, credits, Halyard (revealed later as the city above), Site 6, and Adrian as guarantor/father figure.

I'm continuing the term ledger — Oasis, Mera Vale, Foreman-7, Charter, Lock, Morrow & Sons, Maker's Seal, Covenant band — tracking which characters could plausibly be distinguished from each other (Alex, B11, TJ, Ada, Lock, Tomas) versus ones that blur together (Lina/Suri/Jalen/Ren, Mera/Mara, Nadi/Olani). I'm starting to form a prediction that the father may have died in the mine.

I'm figuring out whether each issue earns a "keep reading" verdict: issue one lands as a tepid yes, issue two is shakier since its cliffhanger (a summons notice) competes with the real hook — the unresolved question of the dad. I'm leaning toward saying yes, but only barely, because the dad mystery is really the only thing pulling a reader forward.

For the "where would a bored classmate put it down" test, I'm weighing page 22 versus page 37 for issue three, trying to figure out which point introduces enough new names and lecture-y exposition to lose a distracted reader.

Actually reconsidering — I think the real drop-off point is page 20, where the story shifts from survival narrative into something more like a lesson, with that "one customer paid... one worker got paid for losing hers" framing. That's exactly where an AI-skeptic reader would smell "educational program" rather than story, so I'll go with page 20 and explain why.

The stage-language lines like "I will remain where the affected people can answer me" and the symmetrical triads — "Industrial flow. Industrial heat. Industrial staff." or "The node sends. The membrane receives. The casing chokes." — read as machine-generated patterning to a skeptical teen. I should be blunt about that in the write-up, keeping it thorough but not overdone.

Read in one sitting, Issue 01 through Issue 03, as assigned homework the night before. I wanted it to be bad. Below is what actually happened to me.

---

## Issue 01: Keel (pages 1–18)

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 1, panel 3.** "Then don't approve it. Just notice it works." I liked him right away. A kid who fixes things and talks back to the rules is a person I can follow.
- **Page 2, the whole page.** This is the hook, and it got me. It's his birthday, he's seventeen, and the gate screen hands him 418,607 credits of his dad's gambling debt. He earned 40 today, it'll take 28.7 years, and he can't travel. Then "Happy birthday, Phantum." The workers going quiet behind him. I stopped looking for reasons to hate it for a second.
- **Page 6.** B11. "Stored. Sleep is more comfortable." / "A fact with a poor record." The robot has a voice, and it's the first character I wanted more of.
- **Page 10, panel 4.** "WAGE FORFEITED: −40 CR" / "That is today's pay." / "I know." Helping the guy costs him the whole day's money, and I already know what 40 means to him because of page 2. That landed.
- **Page 11.** TJ, the dog built out of mine parts, sending its own head through a gap. "That dog yours?" "Recently." Funny.
- **Page 15, panel 1 and page 16, panel 4.** PHYSICAL FLOW 18%, REPORTED FLOW 62%, then it goes up on public screens across Keel. Finally I knew what the story was. Someone is stealing their water and lying about it. That was satisfying.
- **Page 18.** The climb with water rising behind them is a good image to end on.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 3** is a math problem. Thirty, forty-two, fifty-two, fronted, thirty by next shift. I did the sums and still wasn't sure what he bought.
- **Page 4, panel 3.** The grandmother folding and refolding a cloth beside a blue cup. I could tell I was supposed to notice it. I didn't know why, so I moved on.
- **Page 7.** I skimmed the dad's recording. "Bring back the physical reading. Don't trust my conclusion." I didn't know what reading he meant.
- **Pages 15–17.** The hatch, the narrow channel, the conduit, the conduit wall, the ledge, the segment. By the middle of page 16 I'd stopped trying to picture where anyone was standing and just waited for them to get out.

**Page 37.** I open the last issue, the summons from the end of Issue 02 should pay off, and instead I get two new people and paperwork on a table. If I hadn't been assigned this, I'd have stopped here and never reached page 39, which is the best page in the book.

I need to approach this as a blunt, skeptical teen giving a cold read reaction, going issue by issue. Starting with Issue 01: the pump hall repair with a salvaged bracket seems plausible enough, though I'm not sure what this "node" thing is supposed to be — maybe some kind of AI camera — but the line "Then don't approve it. Just notice it works" actually lands well.

The birthday debt reveal is the strongest hook so far — 418,607 credits, 28.7 years, dumped on a seventeen-year-old who inherited his dad's gambling debt. "Happy birthday, Phantum" works, though the name itself feels oddly AI-generated, like something a bot would invent rather than a real name.

Then there's the pharmacy scene with Inez, where a character named Ada shows up out of nowhere with no context — is she an assistant? The whole token/medicine math is confusing too: he's got 52 credits, medicine costs 30, a token costs 42, so he can't afford both and picks medicine, but then Ada apparently fronts him the token anyway, which took two reads to parse. Her line about knowing the route also raises a question I can't answer — what's her actual relationship to him?

The missed payment bit is similarly murky — something about "Site 6" taking his shift and his wages, but it's unclear how that connects to him still missing the payment date after presumably earning credits.

His grandmother's first appearance centers on medicine meant for her, with small sensory details like folded cloth and a blue cup that feel deliberately placed for me to notice. Then there's a sudden reveal of a secret bookcase triggered by placing a book on a shelf, which raises the question of whether she already knew about it — a fun beat, but it comes out of nowhere.

In the workshop scene, the line about building and betting with the same hands lands well, and there's a "lower line" detail tied to a key labeled B11.

The B11 robot scene has genuinely good voice — "Stored. Sleep is more comfortable" and the line about being "a fact with a poor record" — plus a mysterious engraved band reading ADRIAN whose significance isn't yet explained.

The recording scene introduces a confusing plot thread about a "legacy node" and live routing, with lines like "bring back the physical reading, don't trust my conclusion" that I can't quite place yet, and no clarity on who noticed this.

Then Mera and something called "Oasis" show up unexplained — she tries to override a system decision, gets denied, and the system reroutes Alex to Site 6 at 02:14 with the line "let the mechanic reach it," leaving me unsure whether she's meant to be read as an ally or an adversary.

The riddle about pipes and homes feels lost on page 15, and the hatch/channel/conduit geography on page 16 doesn't land either. Mera's motivation is confusing — she opens the segment but denies the homes water, and I barely know Tomas before his fate hits, so the splash ending lands only moderately.

Issue one's core problem: a kid inherits his dad's debt, finds his dad's robot, discovers the city stealing Keel's water, and flees. I'd flag pages 15-16 as the weak spot needing revision.

For issue two, page 19 introduces Halyard and a strong B11 line about "the destination objected," with Ada recovering a packet as Tomas's thread continues.

Then Lock's seal and "charter review" go unexplained, and I'm rereading "they brought the water up with us" twice to parse it. Page 20's Morrow & Sons crate is unclear, and B11's explicit moralizing — "one customer paid for a thing, one worker got paid for losing hers" — feels like the book doing homework for the reader, which students will sense immediately. Page 21 reveals Director Cassian Lock and the surprising detail that dad had 312 patents despite the family being in debt, which is a genuinely interesting hook — his offer to clear the debt pulls the story forward. But page 22's speech with four unmemorable names confuses me on how dad's patents connect to the purifier work of these four people, setting up Lina, Suri, Jalen, and Ren's introductions across pages 23-26.

Those four characters get introduced too fast to tell apart except by their component work, and lines like "Keel's line was diverted, this feeder is contaminated, different failure" and "nobody whose name they kept" need rereading. There's some heist energy with Ren's "take the part, I take the heat" line, and Alex going back is a character moment. Pages 27-28 bring an interesting idea — Houses designing parts not to fit together — plus the oddly specific detail of a thin sleeve at 94%, and some humor with "I expected a longer failure" and "you can have one later." Page 29 argues the purifier is too big and needs industrial staff, making the household smaller, with "less than the House sells, more than Keel gets now" worth rereading. Page 30's B11 moment — "I counted the record and missed the people" — spells out the moral again, on-the-nose but maybe a real growth beat for the character. Then pages 31-32 lose me on who "she" is in the Morrow & Sons order — possibly Mara from page 54 — with "she paid before seeing it" and "she saw the failure list" left confusing.

Pages 33-35 get dense and I skim them — refusing Lock, publishing a public license, registry details. Alex's gain feels unclear since the debt remains and collaborators face reassignment notices as possible punishment, though "they can see us now" suggests some kind of win through open-sourcing, even if Lock's "the Houses will still build it" undercuts the point. Page 36's Mera summons — "let them see who called him" — is a weak cliffhanger since Mera is still unidentified after two issues, more like a notification than real tension. I notice Tomas never gets addressed and Ada nearly vanishes from Issue 2, which I'd summarize as Alex refusing to sell his dad's patents to a corporation while helping workers get credit for their purifier — I'd mark it around page 34. Issue 03 then opens with new names thrown at me immediately, Nadi Ruiz and Clerk Olani in a review room tied to an "orbital industrial branch," leaving me lost about who these people are from the start.

Page 38 introduces Ada's last name, Veyra, and Leona Veyra as a possibly maternal figure with the ambiguous line "I know someone who made it hard to leave" — finally some backstory for Ada. The Leona-Ada reunion on pages 39-40 lands emotionally with lines like "you're taller" and "within a year, and you didn't come," plus Leona's reflection that she saw days she could prevent but not the years she was making, though the "Covenant band" and the band's warming effect remain unexplained. Page 41 reveals Adrian, Leona, and Mera as the three who voted for an emergency authorization with no expiration — seemingly the reveal that the parents created the system, though the delivery is confusing. Page 42 clarifies slightly: the emergency authority was never given an ending, suggesting some AI or system gained permanent power, while "a promise to be seen" I read twice and ultimately let go.

Adrian's restriction on page 43 is a new wrinkle — he wasn't just a gambler but was formally restricted by the system. Mera's guilt surfaces on page 44, and Adrian's death recording on page 45 hits emotionally, with him choosing to stay so the record remains tied to the machine, and his line "Alex, the rest is yours to choose" landing well. Page 46's exchange confirming he was still a gambler but built something worth finding feels genuinely affecting. Pages 47-50 lose me on the mechanics of the lever and "executive designation," though the theme comes through — Alex refuses sole power, and Ada's warning not to make two people the answer for everybody reinforces that no single person should hold it all — but the anticlimactic ending, with debt unchanged and the workshop sealed, risks feeling like a cheat to a teen reader. Page 51 brings relief with Tomas alive, though it reads as a slightly cheap payoff.

I catch Tomas being tied to the gauge callback at 62/18, and the hearing scene where "no instant redistribution occurs" sets up the ending as simply a meeting date rather than resolution. Fourteen months later, confusion creeps in around Morrow & Sons versus Phantum, and whether Mara is a typo for Mera — that name mix-up is worth flagging. The debt barely moving (402,110, down only 16k) feels honestly bleak rather than satisfying, and I'm unclear on what the grandmother's unfolded cloth symbolizes. The ending with Ada tearing the map and the contradictory detail of her keeping the route back to Keel while also stepping into the departure queue is genuinely confusing on a reread. Overall, I don't think I'd pick up the next book.

Beyond that, I'm noting the unresolved loose threads: the grandmother is never named, Ada's relationship to Alex is undefined, Mera's motive is unclear, and the lock device vanishes after issue two. I never learn what the "node" actually is — possibly an AI, but it's never specified. I'm compiling a running ledger of terms as they appear: Keel, node, credits, Halyard (revealed later as the city above), Site 6, and Adrian as guarantor/father figure.

I'm continuing the term ledger — Oasis, Mera Vale, Foreman-7, Charter, Lock, Morrow & Sons, Maker's Seal, Covenant band — tracking which characters could plausibly be distinguished from each other (Alex, B11, TJ, Ada, Lock, Tomas) versus ones that blur together (Lina/Suri/Jalen/Ren, Mera/Mara, Nadi/Olani). I'm starting to form a prediction that the father may have died in the mine.

I'm figuring out whether each issue earns a "keep reading" verdict: issue one lands as a tepid yes, issue two is shakier since its cliffhanger (a summons notice) competes with the real hook — the unresolved question of the dad. I'm leaning toward saying yes, but only barely, because the dad mystery is really the only thing pulling a reader forward.

For the "where would a bored classmate put it down" test, I'm weighing page 22 versus page 37 for issue three, trying to figure out which point introduces enough new names and lecture-y exposition to lose a distracted reader.

Actually reconsidering — I think the real drop-off point is page 20, where the story shifts from survival narrative into something more like a lesson, with that "one customer paid... one worker got paid for losing hers" framing. That's exactly where an AI-skeptic reader would smell "educational program" rather than story, so I'll go with page 20 and explain why.

The stage-language lines like "I will remain where the affected people can answer me" and the symmetrical triads — "Industrial flow. Industrial heat. Industrial staff." or "The node sends. The membrane receives. The casing chokes." — read as machine-generated patterning to a skeptical teen. I should be blunt about that in the write-up, keeping it thorough but not overdone.
